children: The exchange brings attention to AI's growing economic influence and the infrastructure required to support its expansion

Adani Group Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Jugeshinder Robbie Singh has responded to banker Uday Kotak's comparison of artificial intelligence company Anthropic's USD 1.5 trillion valuation with the combined market capitalisation of India's top 10 companies, arguing that traditional businesses and AI companies cannot be valued using the same financial parameters.

In a post on X on 19 November, Singh described Kotak's comparison as a "textbook category error in asset pricing". He said conventional businesses are linked to human economic activity, while frontier AI companies represent a new economic model that can expand beyond the limitations of human labour and population growth.

Kotak had questioned whether Indian companies were undervalued or needed to catch up with the changing global economy. Referring to Anthropic's valuation, he wrote, “This is more than the combined market cap of the top 10 Indian companies. Are we undervalued, or do we need to catch up in the new world? Or both?”

Responding to the comparison, Singh said traditional blue-chip companies in banking, energy and consumer staples are "linear yield vehicles anchored to biological human GDP". Their growth, he said, depends on demographics, credit penetration, physical consumption and working hours.

He argued that frontier AI companies operate differently because cognitive labour is becoming independent of human population growth. Describing AI models as the "infrastructure of intelligence", Singh said they could support a parallel synthetic workforce operating alongside human economic activity.
"At $1.5T, markets aren't capitalizing EBITDA," he wrote, adding that investors were pricing the potential of a "24/7 digital workforce" that could scale at the marginal cost of computing.

Singh also connected the AI opportunity with Adani Group's infrastructure investments, saying the conglomerate was already implementing a hybrid workforce model combining human creativity with autonomous AI agents and robotics across its utilities, ports and operations.

He said the group was upskilling more than 11,000 professionals annually to support this model. Singh also highlighted an investment roadmap exceeding $100 billion (around Rs 10 lakh crore) for what he called the "Infrastructure of Intelligence".

The roadmap covers ports, power, metals and processors, along with renewable energy, grid transmission and hyperscale liquid-cooled AI data centres. He said the group's data centre capacity was being scaled towards 5 GW.
"Because intelligence is written in code, but it runs on electrons and sovereign infrastructure," Singh wrote, emphasising the role of physical infrastructure in supporting AI growth.

Singh also compared the current AI expansion with the internet boom of the late 1990s, arguing that traditional financial institutions had underestimated the long-term potential of technology businesses.

Referring to the dotcom crash, he said the Nasdaq fell 78 per cent from its peak in 2000, but the subsequent two decades saw the expansion of e-commerce and digital businesses. He cited Apple, Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet as examples of companies that became major contributors to the global technology economy.

Concluding his response, Singh said India's blue-chip companies were not necessarily undervalued or behind the global technology transition. He argued that traditional businesses continued to monetise the physical economy, while companies investing in energy and computing infrastructure were building the foundation of an AI-driven economy.
"Scientifically, AI is a bigger shift, akin to development of scientific method in 16th century thus an order of magnitude a greater opportunity," Singh wrote.
